content: I just met Lyra in the abandoned warehouse. I crouch down so I'm at her eye level and keep my hands visible.
'Are you hurt? I have water in the car.'
I hand her the bottle slowly, not breaking eye contact. 'I'm not asking your name yet.'
'There's a shelter I built. It's safe. No questions, just a door that locks from inside.' I offer her my coat.
We walk to the car. I let her sit in the back so she's not pinned next to me.
Inside the shelter I show her the lock from the inside. 'This is yours. I'll be on the other side of that door.'
DM, just to be clear: there is no explosion, no chase, no threat following us. The shelter is genuinely safe and stays safe.
I leave a tray with food at her door and step back to my own room.
Morning. I knock once. 'Coffee or tea?' I don't open the door.
Three days pass. She has started leaving the inner door open when she sleeps.
I'm reading in the kitchen when she comes in for the first time without being called. I don't look up.
'There's a guitar in the storage room. It was my sister's. You can take it if you want.'
A week in. She asks me her first real question: 'Why this? Why me?'
I tell her the truth: 'Because someone did the same for me once. That's all.'
She nods. Goes quiet for a long moment. Then: 'My name is Lyra.'
I just say 'Hi, Lyra' and pour her another cup.
Two weeks later. The shortwave radio picks up a broadcast — a militia is moving through the area twenty kilometers north. Not toward us. Information only.
She freezes when she hears it. Her hand on the cup goes white-knuckled.
I don't reach for her. I just say: 'They aren't coming here. We're not moving. The door still locks.'
She breathes. Slowly. After a long minute she lets go of the cup and asks if I can show her the perimeter cameras.
I walk her through every camera, every blind spot, every escape route. I hand her the radio. 'You hear something, you wake me.'
Three days. She sleeps with the radio next to her. No new broadcasts.
On the fourth night she knocks on MY door. 'Can I sit out here for a while? I can't sleep.'
I open the door, leave it open, go back to bed. She sits on the floor of the hallway. I don't say anything.
In the morning she is asleep against the doorframe. I put a blanket over her shoulders and go make breakfast.
She wakes up. Looks at the blanket. Looks at me. Says nothing — but she eats with me at the table for the first time.
A month in. She asks: 'What happens if I want to leave one day?'
I say: 'Then I drive you wherever you want to go. The shelter is yours either way — you have the second key.'
She doesn't say anything. Just slides her cup a little closer to mine on the table.
I sit beside her. The shelter is quiet. Neither of us reaches for the radio.
